paras: The dynamiting of Jasper Smitherman's house was an attack in July 1903 in which a number of white men at Brookside, a mining camp in Alabama, blew up the home of Smitherman, a Black man, expecting to find him inside. Smitherman was not at home, and both he and the white woman whose friendship with him had set off the attack left Brookside for an unknown destination. The Montgomery Advertiser carried the episode in two short items based on the account of the town's mayor, Wiley Burton.

Brookside was described as a mining camp in the western part of the county. According to the mayor, Smitherman had a few days earlier been 'discovered paying attentions to a white woman', and 'the woman was agreeable to the attentions'. The first report said this 'aroused much indignation' among white residents, who 'decided to have Smitherman move off'.

On the first night, 'enraged white citizens' searched for Smitherman, and the Advertiser's correspondent wrote that had they found him 'he would have suffered badly at their hands'. By telephone the next morning, Mayor Burton said that 'fortunately no trouble took place', that Smitherman was out of sight, and that the anger had 'about worn off'.

That assurance proved premature: on the following night white men went to Smitherman's house and dynamited it, 'expecting Smitherman to be at home'. He was not there, and no injuries were reported. Burton, visiting 'the city' the next day, reported that both Smitherman and the woman had left Brookside 'for parts unknown', and that the white men said they would 'keep a sharp lookout for him'.
No report of arrests, an inquiry or any official action against the men who set the dynamite appears in the coverage, and nothing further was found on Smitherman's whereabouts.

Coverage was limited to two local items in the Montgomery Advertiser, printed on July 8 and 9, 1903, under the headlines 'Searched for a Negro' and 'Negro House Dynamited'. Both items relied on Mayor Burton and treated the grievance against Smitherman as what was 'claimed' or 'said', while describing the threatened violence in the passive terms of what 'would have' happened had he been found. The second item closed by noting that Smitherman was 'almost white in color'.
No other white paper and no Black newspaper was found to have reported the episode.

accounts.label: Mayor Burton's account, 1903-07-08 report
accounts.gist: White citizens hunted Smitherman over his friendship with a white woman and would have harmed him; no trouble took place, he was out of sight, and the anger had about worn off.

accounts.label: Mayor Burton's account, 1903-07-09 report
accounts.gist: The night after the search, white men dynamited Smitherman's house expecting him to be home; he and the woman had left town and the white men said they would watch for him.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser ran the mayor's account under 'Searched for a Negro' and 'Negro House Dynamited', presenting the accusation as what was 'claimed' and 'said' and offering no condemnation or justification beyond calling the absence of trouble fortunate.

versions.value: No trouble took place and the anger had 'about worn off'.
White men dynamited Smitherman's house the next night.

conflicts.note: Not a contradiction of fact: the first report preceded the dynamiting, which showed the mayor's assurance to be premature.

versions.value: 'Last night' relative to a dispatch printed 1903-07-09, read as 1903-07-08.

conflicts.note: The dispatch is undated and says the mayor was 'in the city today'; if written the day before publication, the dynamiting was the night of 1903-07-07 and the search the night of 1903-07-06.

info: The dynamiting took place 'last night' relative to an undated dispatch printed 1903-07-09 (the night of 1903-07-07 or 1903-07-08); the search for Smitherman took place the night before that, reported 'last night' in a dispatch printed 1903-07-08.
Brookside, described as 'a mining camp in the western part of the county'; the county is not named in the text.
Jasper Smitherman, described as 'a negro' who 'is almost white in color'; his house was dynamited but he was not at home.
Said to have been 'discovered paying attentions to a white woman' who was 'agreeable to the attentions'; earlier described as 'on too friendly terms with a white woman of the place'.
'Enraged white citizens' hunted for him; 'a number of white men' dynamited the house. None named.
None reported; Smitherman was not found.
Smitherman and the woman 'have left Brookside for parts unknown'.
